standard_prerequisites.name: Surjection and injection
standard_prerequisites.statement: A function is surjective when every element of the codomain is a value; it is injective when distinct arguments have distinct values; a bijection is both.
standard_prerequisites.use: The constructed g must be shown both surjective and injective (975-978).

standard_prerequisites.name: Definition by recursion
standard_prerequisites.statement: A function whose value at i+1 is computed from the preceding values is well defined by recursion.
standard_prerequisites.use: g(1) = f(1) and g(i+1) = the first value of f not already among g(1), ..., g(i) (963-968).

core_obligations: Define g by recursion: g(1) = f(1), and g(i+1) is the first value of f(1), f(2), ... not already among g(1), ..., g(i), if there is one (963-968).

If A has exactly n elements, g(1), ..., g(n) are all defined and g is a function from {1, ..., n} to A; if A is infinite, some fresh value always exists and g is a function from the positive integers to A (969-974).
Surjectivity: every element of A appears among f(1), f(2), ... because f is surjective, and hence eventually as some g(i) (975-977).
Injectivity: if g(j) = g(i) for j < i then g(i) was already among g(1), ..., g(i-1), contradicting the first-unused rule (977-978).

proof_roadmap.step: Define g by recursion with the first-unused rule.
Split on the size of A to fix the domain of g.
Verify g is surjective and injective.

difficulty_reason: The counted proposition is the author proposition at source lines 912-916: if f from the positive integers to A is surjective, there is a bijection g from Z onto A where Z is either the positive integers or a finite initial segment. The author proof (918-935) defines g by recursion, always taking the first not-yet-used value of f, then runs a case analysis on the size of A and verifies both that g is surjective, using the surjectivity of f, and that g is injective, using the first-unused choice rule. The recursive construction plus the two verifications make this a real argument and not a definition unpacking.
